title: Stage 6: 10M users
scopeHtml: Scope: hybrid timeline fan-out, sharding (range/hash/directory), consistent hashing, SQL vs NoSQL per data type. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Load and goal
notes.html:
Stage 6 goal: Chirp grows from about 1M to 10M registered users, and the two things that were comfortable at Stage 5 (one big Postgres, timelines built by a query) start to hurt. We must now design the timeline properly, shard the data, and stop forcing every data type into one database.

Assumptions for this stage (state your assumptions out loud in an interview):

Quantity Value How we got it
Registered users 10M given
Daily active users (DAU) 4M 40% of registered
Timeline opens per DAU per day 20 feed refreshes
Timeline reads 80M/day = 925/s avg, 2,800/s peak 4M x 20 / 86,400, peak 3x
New posts 2M/day = 23/s avg, 70/s peak 0.5 posts per DAU
Average followers 100 (median 20, a few have 5M) typical social skew
Post row size about 300 B text and metadata id, user, text, counts, time
Post storage growth 2M x 300 B x 365 = about 220 GB/year

What hurts. The Stage 5 home timeline is a query: "get recent posts of everyone I follow, order by time, limit 50". With 100 followees that is a 100-way merge. At 2,800 reads/s peak it is 280k post lookups per second. Replicas help reads, but the primary still takes all writes and its disk grows 220 GB/year plus indexes (about 2x). The table is also a single point where a hot celebrity row can hurt everyone.

Industry examples. Twitter's famous 2012 redesign moved home timelines to Redis lists, precomputed per user (fan-out on write). Instagram sharded Postgres by logical shards early on, with IDs that embed the shard number.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper shop that used to sort every customer's papers when they walk in. At 10M customers you hire someone to sort papers overnight into each customer's bag.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting with "shard everything" before computing the numbers above. At 70 writes/s a single Postgres is not write bound; the issue is read fan-in and size.
  • Forgetting the skew: average followers 100 hides users with 5M followers.

notes.title: Configuration
notes.html:
The Stage 6 target topology. Several data stores, each picked by access pattern, and a fleet sized from the numbers above.

Component Config
API tier 12 x c6i.xlarge (4 vCPU), autoscale 8 to 30 on CPU 55%
Posts DB (SQL) 16 logical shards on 4 x db.r6g.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 64 GB, 2 TB gp3), each with 1 sync standby and 1 read replica
Users/follow graph Postgres, 2 logical shards by user_id hash, db.r6g.xlarge
Timeline cache Redis Cluster, 8 primaries + 8 replicas, cache.r6g.xlarge (26 GB)
Timeline entry sorted by post id, 800 entries per user, 8-byte id plus overhead about 20 B
Counters (likes, retweets) Redis hash with periodic flush to SQL every 5 s
Kafka 3 brokers kafka.m5.large, topic post.created 24 partitions, RF 3, retention 3 days
Fan-out workers 10 pods, consumer group, 2 vCPU each
Celebrity threshold followers > 100,000 means "pull" instead of "push"

Timeline memory check. 4M active users x 800 entries x 20 B = 64 GB. 8 primaries x 26 GB gives 208 GB with headroom (we stay under 60% of memory; Redis needs space for fragmentation and replication buffers).

# Redis cluster excerpt (redis.conf)
maxmemory: 20gb              # of 26 GB node, leaves room for buffers
maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru
cluster-enabled: yes
cluster-node-timeout: 5000   # ms before a node is declared failing
appendonly: no               # timelines are rebuildable, skip AOF cost

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing Redis to exactly the dataset size; replication buffers and fragmentation take 20 to 30%.
  • Turning on AOF for a cache that can be rebuilt from SQL; it slows writes for no gain.

notes.title: Decision and why
notes.html:
Decision 1: hybrid timeline. Push (fan-out on write) for normal users, pull (fan-out on read) for celebrities, merged at read time.

Why: reads outnumber writes about 40 to 1 (925 reads/s vs 23 posts/s). Pre-computing work at write time makes the 40x more common operation a single Redis ZREVRANGE. Fan-out cost is followers x posts: 2M posts x 100 = 200M inserts/day = 2,300/s average, 7,000/s peak, easy for 10 workers pipelining into Redis. But one post by a 5M-follower account is 5M inserts; do that at 5 posts a day and a celebrity alone costs 25M inserts, and a burst clogs the queue. So we skip pushing for accounts over 100k followers and merge their recent posts in at read time.

Decision 2: shard posts by hash of post_id or by user_id? We shard by user_id hash (author). Fetching "an author's profile page" is one shard; timelines are served from Redis so cross-author reads are rare. Post ids are Snowflake-style (41 bits time, 10 bits shard/worker, 12 bits sequence), so ids sort by time and carry no central sequence.

Decision 3: SQL vs NoSQL per data type.

Data Store Why
Users, auth, settings Postgres relational, transactions, small
Follow graph Postgres (two tables, follower->followee and the reverse) needed in both directions; 10M x 100 = 1B edges, about 16 B each = 16 GB
Posts Postgres shards structured, secondary indexes, moderate write rate
Timelines Redis sorted/ list tiny rows, extreme read rate, rebuildable
Counters Redis, flushed hot increments would lock rows
Media metadata Postgres; blobs on S3 (Stage 7)

We do not use Cassandra yet: the write rate (70/s) does not need it, and keeping posts in SQL keeps joins and moderation queries simple. Twitter and Instagram stayed on MySQL/Postgres for the core tables long past this scale.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing NoSQL "for scale" with a 70 writes/s workload.
  • Pushing to every follower including celebrities, then being surprised by queue lag.

notes.title: Alternatives (branches)
notes.html:
Branch A: Timeline design

Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull) Hybrid
Read cost O(1): one Redis range O(followees) merge O(1) plus a few celebrity merges
Write cost O(followers) per post O(1) normal users push, celebs skip
Storage 800 entries x all active users none extra same as push
Freshness seconds of fan-out lag instant seconds for push, instant for celeb
Worst case 5M-follower post read of 2,000 followees bounded both sides
Who uses it early Twitter early Facebook-style feeds, small apps modern Twitter, Instagram feeds

Choose hybrid. Pure push dies on celebrities; pure pull wastes CPU on the 40x more frequent operation. Cost: complexity (two paths, a threshold, merge logic).

Inactive users. Do not fan out to users who have not logged in for 30 days; rebuild their timeline on first open (a pull). This cuts fan-out writes by roughly 40% in a typical app.

Branch B: Sharding strategy

Range Hash Directory
Placement user_id 1 to 1M on shard 1 hash(user_id) mod N lookup table user -> shard
Range scans great impossible across shards per entry
Hot spots newest range gets all new writes even controllable per user
Resharding split a range, easy mod N moves almost everything move one user at a time
Extra moving part none none lookup service must be HA

Choose hash with many logical shards (16) mapped to few physical hosts (4), and keep the logical to physical map in config. Resharding then means moving a whole logical shard to a new host (a file-level copy), never re-hashing rows. A directory is the escape hatch for a few giant tenants.

Branch C: Consistent hashing for the cache tier

hash(key) mod N is catastrophic for caches: going from 8 to 9 nodes remaps about 8/9 of keys, the cache goes cold and the database takes the full load. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring; adding a node moves only about 1/N of keys.

Ring (0 to 2^32), 3 nodes with 100 virtual nodes each
   key K hashes to a point, owner = next node clockwise
   add node D: only keys between D's predecessor and D move (about 1/4)
   virtual nodes smooth the load: 100 per node keeps imbalance under about 10%

Redis Cluster actually uses 16,384 fixed hash slots (CRC16 of key mod 16384) assigned to nodes, a close cousin: moving slots between nodes moves only those keys. Memcached clients (ketama) use true consistent hashing; DynamoDB and Cassandra use it internally.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "consistent hashing" without virtual nodes; a 3-node ring without vnodes is unbalanced.
  • Using range sharding by created_at; all new writes hit one shard.
  • Forgetting cross-shard queries (global search, counts) need another system (Stage 7).

notes.title: What breaks next
notes.html:
Walk the bottlenecks as the user count heads to 50M.

  1. Search. ILIKE '%word%' across 16 shards is hopeless. Needs a search engine (Stage 7).
  2. Media. Image uploads through app servers saturate NICs and CPU for resizing. Needs a pipeline with object storage.
  3. Abuse and bursts. One scripted client can issue 10k requests/s. Needs rate limiting and a gateway.
  4. Monolith deploy coupling. 30 engineers in one repo; a bad deploy takes out everything. When to split, and when not to, is Stage 7.
  5. Hot keys. A viral post's counter in one Redis slot gets 50k INCR/s. Mitigation: shard the counter into 16 sub-keys and sum on read.
  6. Fan-out lag. Kafka consumer lag metric above 30 s means users see stale feeds; alert on consumer_lag_seconds.

Common interview traps.

  • Not naming a metric: the fan-out health signal is consumer lag, not CPU.
  • Ignoring the cold-cache event after a Redis failure: all 4M timelines rebuild at once and hammer SQL. Rebuild lazily with a rate limit.

notes.title: Cost
notes.html:
Approximate monthly on-demand AWS us-east-1 (prices change; confirm on the pricing page):

Item Count x unit Monthly
API servers 12 x c6i.xlarge at about $125 $1,500
Posts Postgres 4 hosts x 3 instances (primary, standby, replica) of db.r6g.2xlarge at about $700 $8,400
User/graph Postgres 2 shards x 3 x db.r6g.xlarge at about $350 $2,100
Redis 16 x cache.r6g.xlarge at about $300 $4,800
Kafka 3 brokers + storage $1,200
Fan-out workers 10 x 2 vCPU $600
Load balancer, CDN, egress, S3, monitoring $5,000
Total about $23,600/month, roughly $2.4 per 1,000 registered users

Reserved instances (1 year) typically cut the compute part 30 to 40%. Cost per DAU is about $0.006/month.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating only compute; network egress and replicas are often 30% of the bill.
  • Not noticing that Postgres replicas dominate the cost: a read replica per shard doubles it.

notes.title: LLD view
notes.html:
Inside the service the timeline concern becomes an interface, so push, pull and hybrid can be swapped.

interface TimelineService {
    List<PostId> home(UserId u, Cursor c, int limit);
}

class HybridTimelineService implements TimelineService {
    private final TimelineStore pushed;     // Redis ZSET per user
    private final FollowGraph graph;
    private final PostRepository posts;     // sharded
    private static final int CELEB = 100_000;

    public List<PostId> home(UserId u, Cursor c, int limit) {
        List<PostId> base = pushed.range(u, c, limit);
        List<UserId> celebs = graph.followedCelebrities(u); // cached
        List<PostId> extra = posts.recentByAuthors(celebs, c, limit);
        return mergeByIdDesc(base, extra, limit);           // ids sort by time
    }
}

final class ShardRouter {
    private final int logicalShards = 16;
    int shardOf(long userId) { return (int) ((userId * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15L >>> 33) % logicalShards); }
}

Fan-out worker: idempotent per (post_id, follower_id) (a Redis ZADD of the same member is a no-op), so Kafka redelivery is safe. Cursor pagination uses the last post id, not an offset, because new posts shift offsets.

Common interview traps.

  • Offset pagination on a timeline: duplicates and gaps as new posts arrive.
  • Non-idempotent fan-out causing duplicate entries after a consumer restart.

notes.title: Decision gravity
notes.html:
Decision Gravity Why
Hybrid timeline Reversible (two-way) Timelines are derived; you can switch the threshold or rebuild from posts
Redis for timelines Reversible Cache of truth in SQL
Hash sharding of posts by user_id One-way door Changing the shard key means rewriting every row and every query that assumed it
Snowflake ids with shard bits One-way door Ids are embedded in URLs, caches and other systems
16 logical shards Mostly one-way, but cheap to increase if you planned for it (split 16 into 32) Choose more logical shards than you need today
Postgres vs Cassandra for posts Semi-reversible Migration needs dual writes, weeks of work
Celebrity threshold Reversible, a config value

The rule: derived data is a two-way door, the source-of-truth shard key and id format are one-way.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking a shard key without checking the top 3 queries.
  • Calling sharding reversible; it is a data migration project.

notes.title: Concepts learned
notes.html:
• Fan-out on write, on read, and hybrid; the celebrity problem
  • Read vs write ratio as the lever for precomputation
  • Sharding: range vs hash vs directory; logical vs physical shards
  • Consistent hashing, virtual nodes, Redis hash slots
  • Snowflake ids, cursor pagination, idempotent consumers
  • Polyglot persistence: choosing SQL, Redis, Kafka per data type
  • Consumer lag as a health metric

Common interview traps.

  • Listing concepts without tying each to a number or a failure.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• At 10M users the home timeline query and the single primary are the pain; reads are 40x writes, so precompute.
  • Hybrid fan-out: push for normal users, pull and merge for accounts above about 100k followers, skip inactive users.
  • Shard posts by hashed user_id into 16 logical shards on 4 hosts; ids embed the shard (Snowflake).
  • Consistent hashing or hash slots keep cache node changes from cold-starting everything.
  • SQL for users, graph, posts; Redis for timelines and counters; Kafka for fan-out; Cassandra not yet needed.
  • About $24k/month. One-way doors: shard key and id format. Everything derived is rebuildable.
